reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The closest official measure of AI use in this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Other services, the NAICS 81 grouping that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, 15.0% answered yes in the latest period, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The series first asked the question in September 2023, and the Census Bureau suppresses some values, marked S. Nonprofits are not a standalone line in that survey, so the figure is a proxy for the sector rather than a count of charities, and it should be read that way.

On what the technology is actually used for, Candid, the nonprofit data organization behind GuideStar and Foundation Center, points to the donor side: donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities, which means many will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter. The Center for Effective Philanthropy examines how foundations and nonprofits deploy AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. NTEN, the Nonprofit Technology Network, runs sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption. The practical territory these sources describe is grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets.

The organisational ecosystem is thin. The World of AI catalogues four individually verified organisations in its nonprofits and open source foundations category, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, each classified against a document the organisation published about itself. LMSYS is the most directly AI-central, stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used to benchmark model quality. Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education rather than a producer. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, though their missions predate AI. None are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense, and the catalogue notes no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights. Candid tracks the funding side, including grantmaking trends and funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure.

The access gap gets explicit attention. The AI Equity Project builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, turning public libraries and community spaces into learning environments where senior citizens and student volunteers explore practical AI tools together. It operates as a global network providing standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities, and runs the International AI for Impact Challenge, where top participants secure engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advisement. NTEN frames the same problem as inequity within organizations and across the sector, and argues that users, builders, and funders all carry responsibility for equitable technology use. Its responses include an Equity Guide practitioners can pledge to use, scholarships for courses and certificates, and recognition of open source developers building tools for nonprofit and advocacy groups.

On risk and regulation the harvested material is largely silent. NTEN tracks AI policy adoption among nonprofits, and governance capacity is named as the constraint on the sector's work, but none of these pages sets out a regulatory regime, a compliance obligation, or a liability finding specific to nonprofits. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index is cited as the macro series reporting AI's social impact and implementation across mission-driven and public-sector organizations, which is where a reader would look for broader trend data rather than sector-specific rules.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a few modest conclusions. Measured adoption is real but low, at 15.0% of firms in the Census Bureau's Other services grouping, and it moved only from 13.7% in the prior period, so this is not a sector in rapid transformation. The binding constraints the sources name are budget and governance capacity, not model access. Donor behavior is shifting toward AI-mediated research, which changes how a nonprofit is found before any internal tooling decision is made. And the supporting ecosystem of nonprofit and open-source AI organisations is small enough to be catalogued in four entries, so a nonprofit looking for shared infrastructure or neutral evaluation capacity will find little of it in the nonprofit sector itself.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The World of AI's catalogue lists four individually verified organisations in this category ,  two nonprofits and two open-source foundations ,  each carrying a classification note sourced to a document the organisation published about itself, with the source and the date it was last read recorded. The page describes LMSYS as the most directly AI-central entry, stewarding Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform the wider AI community uses to benchmark model quality, and notes that such neutral evaluation sits outside the commercial incentives of the labs being assessed. Khan Academy is characterised as an end-user of AI capability in education rather than a producer, while the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, though their missions predate AI. The page states that none of the four are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense, and that it covers no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-centre specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights. It adds that the notes confirm only organisational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access or governance detail.
